title: RBAC v2 in Private Deployments — installer + admin workflows, cluster scoping, IdP constraints (working notes)
body:
Context
- Private deployments are trending toward regulated environments where customers insist on:
  - Least-privilege roles (separation of duties) across platform admin vs security admin vs operator
  - Proof that authorization is enforced consistently (deny-by-default)
  - Auditable admin actions and ability to export audit logs to SIEM
  - Customer-managed IdP constraints (SAML/SCIM group naming, limited claims, sometimes no SCIM)
- This doc is working notes for how RBAC v2 semantics apply specifically to Private: installer/bootstrap, cluster scoping, and how we survive “weird IdP” realities.

Non-goals (for this doc)
- Not rewriting the overall RBAC v2 model (see Confluence design overview)
- Not defining every permission string (see permission inventory)
- Not committing to full ABAC/custom policy language

Key Private-specific assumptions
1) There is a “control plane” running inside the customer environment (or a customer-managed VPC) with some Redwood components.
2) Identity is customer-controlled. We may receive:
   - A user identity with group claims OR
   - A service principal identity OR
   - A “break-glass” local admin mechanism if IdP is down
3) Private has a natural additional scope axis: cluster (and sometimes region/site), because a given customer org might have multiple clusters (prod/stage, different data centers, or for residency).

Terminology (Private)
- Cluster: a specific Private installation (or logical cluster) with its own runtime/control plane.
- Environment: customer concept (prod/stage/dev) that may map to clusters 1:1 or N:1 depending on topology.
- Bootstrap admin: initial RBAC principal who can bind roles and map IdP groups.

Open questions we must resolve early
- Is “cluster” a first-class scope in RBAC v2 or represented as environment scope? (Current leaning: cluster is explicit for Private because installer/bootstrap needs it and audit scoping is clearer.)
- How do we represent a user who should be able to administer ONLY cluster A but not cluster B in the same org?
- What happens when IdP group claims exceed header/cookie size (Azure AD can get large)?
- What’s our story when the customer cannot provide stable group IDs (only names) or uses nested groups?

Installer / bootstrap flow (target)
Goal: A fresh Private install must come up secure-by-default, with minimal but sufficient access to complete setup, without requiring Redwood staff to be global admins.

Proposed steps
A) Install time (day 0)
- Installer generates a bootstrap configuration artifact:
  - bootstrap principal: either
    1) A customer-provided IdP group (recommended) OR
    2) A one-time bootstrap token/certificate tied to a local admin user (fallback)
  - scope: cluster=<this-cluster-id>
  - bindings: assign built-in role template “Private Bootstrap Admin” (see below)
- Installer writes this into control plane storage (or sealed secret depending on mode).

B) First login / first API call
- Bootstrap admin can:
  - Configure IdP mapping (group -> role binding) for ongoing access
  - Create additional role bindings and remove bootstrap access once stable
  - Configure audit log export target (if included in Private package)
- We should strongly nudge user to:
  - Create at least 2 admins (to avoid lockout)
  - Set up break-glass procedure with security controls

C) Post-bootstrap hardening
- Bootstrap role binding should be time-bound (default 7 days?) OR at least explicitly flagged in UI.
- Console should show a “bootstrap access still enabled” banner.

Why bootstrap is tricky
- Some customers insist that no local-only accounts exist (everything must go through IdP).
- Some customers cannot provide group claims until after app registration / SP is approved (chicken-and-egg).
- Air-gapped installs may not have live IdP connectivity during initial setup.

Current compromise
- Support both bootstrap via IdP group and fallback local bootstrap token.
- Make local bootstrap token “break-glass-grade”: short TTL, single-use, loudly logged, and optionally requires dual-control (see break-glass notes).

Role templates (Private-specific)
We need Private opinionated defaults because customers ask “what roles should we create?”

Candidate templates (draft)
1) Private Platform Admin (cluster-scoped)
- Intended: the team that operates the Private platform cluster(s)
- Can:
  - Manage deployments/runtime config within a cluster (scaling, routing policy at cluster level)
  - View cluster health/metrics
  - Manage model availability/pinning within cluster (but NOT org-wide identity)
- Cannot:
  - Change IdP settings
  - Export audit logs unless explicitly granted (depends on customer separation-of-duties)

2) Private Security Admin (org-scoped, but may also need cluster read)
- Intended: security team
- Can:
  - Manage org/users/roles/role bindings
  - Configure audit log export and retention policies
  - Manage break-glass approvals (if workflow exists)
- Cannot:
  - Change runtime routing policies (unless customer wants security to have that power)

3) Private Deployment Operator (cluster-scoped)
- Intended: on-call operators / SRE-equivalent
- Can:
  - Restart services, rotate service tokens, manage certificates (where exposed)
  - View logs/diagnostics
  - Execute “safe operations” playbook actions
- Cannot:
  - Change RBAC mappings, role templates, or audit export

4) Private Read-only Auditor (org + cluster read)
- Intended: internal audit / compliance
- Can:
  - Read configuration (RBAC, routing policies, retention settings)
  - Read audit logs + export (if that’s their job)
- Cannot:
  - Make changes

5) Private Bootstrap Admin (cluster-scoped + limited org bootstrap)
- Intended: initial setup only
- Needs:
  - Manage identity mappings and role bindings
  - View / configure system integrations required for setup
- Should be explicitly “temporary” in UI and docs

NOTE: We need to align with rbac-policy-bundle PR-201 so template naming is stable and permissions are consistent.

Scope model for Private
We need to answer: “What is the smallest thing you can grant access to?”

Proposed scope axes
- org scope: actions affecting identity, billing (if applicable), global settings, audit export policies
- project scope: may or may not exist in Private; some customers segment by project/team (optional)
- environment scope: user-facing segmentation (prod/stage)
- cluster scope: concrete installation

Option 1 (recommended): Add cluster as a scope type
- Pros:
  - Clear mapping to installer/bootstrap and operational ownership
  - Clean separation if customer has multiple clusters per org
  - Audit log scoping becomes straightforward: resource_scope=cluster:<id>
- Cons:
  - Extra complexity for Hosted semantics (but Hosted can ignore cluster)
  - Role binding UI needs to handle another scope type

Option 2: Map cluster to environment
- Pros:
  - Reuse “environment” scope everywhere
- Cons:
  - Breaks down when env != cluster (common in Private)
  - Harder to reason about break-glass and cluster-limited operations

Action item
- Confirm with Jordan/Ines: cluster as first-class scope in evaluator + bindings storage, even if hosted rarely uses it.

Customer-managed IdP constraints (what we’re seeing)
Observed patterns (from POC calls / SE notes)
- Some customers only send group names, not immutable group IDs.
- Some have nested groups and expect “user is in group X (including nested)” semantics.
- Some cap the number of groups in the token and require “app roles” instead.
- Some don’t want SCIM; provisioning is manual and via group membership only.
- Some require that service-to-service calls use a non-human principal with minimal privileges.

Implications for RBAC v2
- We should avoid “role binding by user email” as primary; group-based bindings are more scalable.
- We need a stable “subject identifier” in authz logs that the customer recognizes (user principal name, group, etc.).
- If nested groups aren’t expanded by IdP in the token, we can’t reliably expand them without calling back to IdP (not acceptable for air-gapped / latency). Therefore:
  - Requirement: customer must configure IdP to include effective groups OR we support “app roles” / “roles” claims.

Minimum IdP contract (Private)
- Must provide:
  - user_id (stable)
  - org identifier (tenant)
  - one of: groups OR roles claim
- Nice to have:
  - group IDs (immutable) not just names
  - email

Fallbacks when group claims are too large
- Recommend: app roles claim (small list)
- Or: configure IdP to send only groups relevant to Redwood application
- We should document a “token too large / too many groups” troubleshooting guide

Console UX expectations in Private
Private customers will use Console heavily for admin flows; also some will be API-only.

MVP flows that must work (Private)
- View role bindings for a cluster
- Assign role template to IdP group at cluster scope
- Verify “who am I” + “what permissions do I have?”
- “Why was I denied?” should show denial reason and missing permission (admin-only debug)
- Bootstrap banner + guided setup checklist (at least link to docs)

Access recovery / break-glass (Private)
Private is where break-glass actually matters because:
- IdP outages happen and customers still need to restore service
- Misconfigured role bindings can lock out all admins

Principles
- Break-glass must be:
  - Explicitly enabled by customer
  - Time-bound
  - Audited + alerted
  - Hard to use accidentally

Possible mechanisms (to align with Security)
1) Local break-glass account
- Disabled by default; can be enabled with a physical/operational procedure
- Customer controls credentials (stored in their vault)

2) One-time elevation token
- Requires two-person approval (customer side) + optionally Redwood support involvement (but we should not require Redwood)
- Token grants “BreakGlassAdmin” role binding for N hours

3) Kubernetes-level access as ultimate fallback
- For air-gapped clusters, cluster-admin at k8s can edit the control plane DB/CRDs
- We should document this as the “last resort” with warnings

We must ensure audit log captures break-glass usage
- authz decision logs should include a flag like subject.is_break_glass=true
- all actions during break-glass window should be traceable

Service accounts in Private
Customers want non-human identities:
- CI/CD pipeline to deploy model/routing changes
- Monitoring system to pull metrics
- Audit exporter to ship logs

Needs
- Service principals that can be bound to roles, same as users/groups
- Rotation story (keys/certs) and permission separation
- Ability to restrict service account to a cluster (not org-wide)

Migration notes (RBAC v1 -> v2) specifically for Private
Risks in Private
- Customers may have heavily customized operational runbooks around existing coarse roles.
- Private upgrades may lag Hosted, so we must support long dual-read windows.
- Lockouts are higher severity (customer may not have quick Redwood intervention).

Mitigations
- Pre-upgrade validation:
  - compute “would deny” report in dry-run mode (dual-read) before enforcement
  - surface missing permissions for existing admin groups
- Provide a documented default mapping:
  - Old “admin” -> Private Platform Admin + Security Admin (or combined) depending on previous behavior
- Installer upgrade step should include a “confirm admin principal” prompt

Telemetry / validation we should add (Private)
- authz deny rate by endpoint + by scope type
- count of requests evaluated using cached decision vs live evaluation
- number of “unscoped” requests (should be near zero; scoping bugs show here)
- number of unrecognized group/role claims

Private-specific edge cases
1) Multiple clusters, shared IdP
- Same user should have different roles per cluster
- UI needs cluster selector and clear scope display

2) Shared operations team across multiple customer subsidiaries
- Might require org-of-org model (out of scope) OR multiple orgs with same IdP; we need a clean story for “same user in multiple orgs”.

3) Air-gapped installs
- No external calls for policy evaluation.
- No dependency on cloud control plane for authz decisions.

4) Time skew
- If tokens have exp/nbf and cluster time is off, auth failures look like authz issues.
- Installer should include NTP/time sanity check (note to private installer team).

Action items / TODOs
- [Jordan] confirm scope model includes cluster scope and how it’s represented in policy evaluator API (string format, normalization)
- [Ines] validate tenancy model: org->cluster binding and how we prevent cross-cluster access by mistake
- [Kaitlyn] draft minimum IdP claim contract for Private and troubleshooting for large group claims
- [Colin] collect 3–5 real customer IdP configurations (sanitized) for docs and QA
- [Vivek] align role template names + descriptions with policy-bundle generator (avoid renames in docs)
- [Marcus] confirm break-glass mechanism acceptable for SOC2 evidence + enterprise questionnaires
- [Ethan] verify control plane endpoints that must be cluster-scoped vs org-scoped and ensure annotations align

Notes to self (unresolved)
- We need to decide where “audit log export configuration” lives in scope terms: org-scoped with cluster destinations? or cluster-scoped? Customers asked for per-cluster export targets.
- Routing policy edits: in Private, some customers treat routing as production change management and want strict separation (operator can apply pre-approved policy but cannot author it). This might require splitting permissions: routing_policy.write vs routing_policy.apply.
- Private installer should probably print a post-install summary including:
  - cluster id
  - bootstrap binding subject (group or token id)
  - link to Console setup page
  - break-glass disabled/enabled status

Appendix: Example role binding statements (pseudo)
- Bind IdP group “redwood-private-platform-admins” to role PrivatePlatformAdmin at scope cluster:cluster-prod-1
- Bind IdP group “redwood-private-security-admins” to role PrivateSecurityAdmin at scope org:ironbank
- Bind service principal “audit-exporter” to role AuditExporter at scope cluster:cluster-prod-1

Appendix: Questions for upcoming customer POC (Northbridge)
- Do you have multiple clusters planned (prod/stage or different sites)?
- Can you include group IDs in the assertion/token?
- Can you restrict groups emitted to application-specific groups?
- Do you need separate admins for identity vs operations?
- How do you want break-glass handled (local account vs token vs k8s-only)?
